title: WITNEY v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary: In the case of Witney v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Witney, a British citizen identifying as a Gypsy by birth and thus falling within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers, brought a complaint against the United Kingdom. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities facing barriers to maintaining their traditional lifestyle due to planning regulations and a shortage of authorised sites. Mr. Witney and his wife, after years of travelling and experiencing harassment both from other Travellers and the police, sought to settle on their own land in Buckinghamshire for health and family reasons. Despite purchasing land and applying for planning permission to live in a mobile home there, his application was refused on environmental and planning grounds, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful. Mr. Witney argued that these decisions interfered with his rights under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (respect for private and family life), as well as Article 6 (right to a fair hearing), Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). However, following the European Court’s judgment in Buckley v. the United Kingdom, which found no violation in a similar context, Mr. Witney withdrew his application, and the case was struck out. This case reflects the ongoing challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in securing lawful residence and recognition of their cultural needs, particularly in the context of restrictive planning policies in the United Kingdom during the 1990s.
